title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence After at Most K Operations
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase letters and an integer `k`. One operation picks a position of `s` and moves its letter one step forward or one step back in the alphabet, which is circular: one step forward from `'z'` is `'a'`, and one step back from `'a'` is `'z'`. You may perform at most `k` operations in total, on any positions (the same position may be changed several times).

Return the greatest possible length of a palindromic subsequence of the string after the operations. A subsequence keeps some of the characters in their original order; they need not be next to each other.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Without operations this is the classic longest palindromic subsequence, an interval DP: for `s[i..j]`, drop `s[i]`, drop `s[j]`, or wrap both ends around the best answer for `s[i + 1..j - 1]`. Trying all 2^n subsequences is hopeless for 200 letters.

Only kept letters need operations. A middle letter is free, and a pair becomes equal after `min(gap, 26 - gap)` operations, where `gap` is their alphabet distance (the short way may wrap past `'z'`). So the budget becomes a third dimension: the best length in `s[i..j]` with at most `c` operations.

## Approach

1. Fill the starts `i` from right to left. Row `i` needs only row `i + 1`, kept in `prev`.
2. `dp[i][c] = 1` for every budget: one letter is a palindrome.
3. For each end `j > i`, compute `cost`, the operations that make `s[i]` and `s[j]` equal.
4. For each budget `c`, take the better of `dropFirst[c]` (for `s[i + 1..j]`) and `dropLast[c]` (for `s[i..j - 1]`); if `cost <= c`, pairing the ends gives `inside[c - cost] + 2`.
5. After the last row, `prev[n - 1][k]` is the answer for the whole string.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abced"`, `k = 2`; each row lists `dp[j][0..2]`.

- `i = 3`: `"ed"` costs 1 to pair, so `dp[4] = [1, 2, 2]`.
- `i = 2`: `"ce"` costs 2: `[1, 1, 2]`. In `"ced"` the ends `'c'`, `'d'` cost 1 and surround `'e'`, so `inside[0] + 2 = 3` and `dp[4] = [1, 3, 3]`.
- `i = 1`: `"bced"` pairs `'b'`, `'d'` for 2, but `inside[0] + 2` is only 3, the same as `dropFirst`: `[1, 3, 3]`.
- `i = 0`: `'a'` and `'d'` are 3 apart, too many, so `dp[4] = [1, 3, 3]` again.

The answer is `prev[4][2] = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · k): each pair `i < j` handles every budget once.
- Space: O(n · k): two rows instead of a full `n × n × (k + 1)` table.

## Pitfalls

- The alphabet wraps: `'a'` and `'z'` are 1 apart, so the cost is `min(gap, 26 - gap)`, not `gap`.
- Only pairs cost operations; the middle letter of an odd-length palindrome is free.
- When `j = i + 1` the inside is empty; `prev[i]` holds zeros for it.
- `dp[j - 1]` belongs to the row being built, so `j` must grow upward.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `i`, `j` | start and end of the interval `s[i..j]` |
| `dp` | row `i`: `dp[j][c]` is the best length in `s[i..j]` with at most `c` operations |
| `prev` | the same row for start `i + 1` |
| `gap`, `cost` | alphabet distance of `s[i]` and `s[j]`, and the operations that make them equal |
| `dropFirst`, `dropLast`, `inside` | the answers for `s[i + 1..j]`, `s[i..j - 1]` and `s[i + 1..j - 1]` |
| `c` | the operation budget |
